newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, CEPA to discuss power plant deal--CEPA.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, CEPA to discuss power plant deal--CEPA.

text.p: The Pakistani authorities on Monday invited the Hong Kong-based Consolidated Power of Asia Ltd (CEPA) for talks on a troubled $5.5 billion power plant deal, a company official said.
CEPA resident director in Pakistan Latif Chaudhry told Reuters the invitation had come from the government's Private Power and Infrastructure Board (PPIB), which deals with private power projects.

The government said last month it had decided in principle to terminate the 1995 deal for the project in the southern province of Sindh on the ground that the power it produced would be very expensive.
The government said it wanted to cancel the deal, which CEPA had made with the previous government of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, by "mutual agreement".
Chaudhry said the PPIB letter "does not indicate any such decision" by the government.
There was no immediate information about when the negotiations would be held.

While CEPA has been seeking meetings with government leaders to explain its position, Bhutto threatened to go to court to defend the project, saying moves to terminate the deal discriminated against Sindh, her home province.
Under the agreement, CEPA was to build eight 660-megawatt coal-based thermal power plants at Keti Bunder, about 60 km (37 miles) west of the port city of Karachi.

CEPA, in which U.S. power giant Southern Co has an 80 percent stake and Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings Ltd 20 percent, also had plans to develop a 14-metre (46-foot) deep sea port in Sindh and to set up a special industrial zone at the site at a total cost of $1.0 billion.
